_README.purpose: Hand-curated source material for BookSphere content. Nothing in this file is generated.
_README.why_it_is_hand_written: The strategy forbids fabricated quotations and invented endorsements, and a language model will produce both fluently and confidently. 'Bill Gates called this his favourite book' is the exact shape of a sentence that gets invented. So quotes and notable references are written by hand, and each carries a verify field that the generator prints as a pre-publish checklist.

fields.quote: A short line from the book. Kept brief on purpose - fair use, not an excerpt.
fields.quote_note: Anything that changes how the quote should be presented, e.g. a translation or an author quoting someone else.
fields.core_idea: The one idea worth understanding first, in plain language. Original phrasing, never the publisher's copy.
fields.tension: The argument inside the book - the thing reasonable people land on differently. Feeds Pillar F.
fields.misses: What typical summaries flatten. Feeds Pillar H.
fields.apply: One realistic action someone could take today. Feeds Pillar D.
fields.notable: A documented public reference by a well-known person. OMIT ENTIRELY rather than guess.
fields.verify: What a human must confirm before this is published.
fields.takeaways: Four to six things a reader can actually use. Feeds the numbered-list pillar, where the hook promises a count and every slide has to deliver one of them. Written by hand: a numbered promise the carousel does not keep is worse than no hook at all.

_README.rule: If you cannot name where a claim comes from, delete the claim. An empty field costs nothing; an invented one costs the account.

books.title: Atomic Habits
books.author: James Clear
books.quote: You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.
books.core_idea: Behaviour follows design more reliably than it follows intention. The lever is the environment and the size of the first step, not the strength of the commitment.
books.tension: Discipline or environment? The book argues that willpower is the least reliable input, which is uncomfortable if you believe effort is the point.
books.misses: Most summaries reduce it to 1% better every day. The more useful half is the argument that identity precedes behaviour: you act like the person you already believe you are.
books.apply: Take one habit you keep failing at and change one physical thing about where it happens. Move the object closer, or move the obstacle further away.
books.verify: Quote is widely printed and appears in the book's opening chapters. Confirm wording against your copy before posting.
takeaways: Make it obvious. Put the cue where you will trip over it, not where it is tidy.
Shrink the first move until it is embarrassing. Two minutes, not twenty.
Never miss twice. One skipped day is noise; two is the start of a new pattern.
Change the room before you change the resolve. Distance does the work willpower cannot.
Decide who you are becoming, then let each action cast a vote for that person.

books.title: The Psychology of Money
books.author: Morgan Housel
books.quote: Doing well with money has a little to do with how smart you are and a lot to do with how you behave.
books.core_idea: Financial outcomes are driven by behaviour under uncertainty, not by intelligence or technical skill. Two people with the same information routinely get opposite results.
books.tension: Save aggressively or live now? The book refuses to resolve it, arguing that the right answer depends on what you are actually optimising for.
books.misses: Summaries lift the compounding chapter and drop the one about luck and risk, which is the part that changes how you judge other people's outcomes.
books.apply: Write down the last financial decision you made and name whether it was skill or timing. Most people cannot tell, which is the point.
books.verify: Quote appears in the introduction. Confirm wording.
takeaways: Nobody is crazy. Every financial decision makes sense given the life that produced it.
Luck and risk are the same force seen from opposite ends. Judge process, not outcome.
Enough is a number you set. Without it, every gain resets the target.
Wealth is what you do not see: the cars unbought, the upgrades declined.
Room for error is not pessimism. It is what lets you stay in the game long enough to compound.

books.title: Man's Search for Meaning
books.author: Viktor E. Frankl
books.quote: When we are no longer able to change a situation, we are challenged to change ourselves.
books.quote_note: Translated from German - wording differs between editions. Say 'in one translation' if quoting precisely matters.
books.core_idea: Meaning is found rather than assigned, and can be found in work, in love, or in the attitude taken toward unavoidable suffering.
books.tension: The memoir is what people remember; the clinical second half is where the argument actually lives, and it resists the self-help framing the book usually gets.
books.misses: It is quoted as inspiration and read as a survival story, but it is a clinical argument about a therapeutic method.
books.apply: Name one situation you cannot currently change, and one thing about your response to it that you can.
books.verify: Translation-dependent. Check your edition's wording before printing it on a card.
takeaways: Meaning is found rather than assigned. It is discovered in a situation, not chosen in the abstract.
There are three routes: what you make, who you love, and the stance you take toward unavoidable suffering.
The last freedom is the choice of response, and it survives conditions that take everything else.
A why makes a how bearable. Without one, comfort does not compensate.
Chasing happiness directly tends to lose it. It arrives as a by-product of something pursued for its own sake.

books.title: The Hard Thing About Hard Things
books.author: Ben Horowitz
books.quote: There are no silver bullets, only lead bullets.
books.core_idea: The decisions that matter most are the ones where every option is bad, and there is no framework that makes them not bad.
books.tension: Most business books present decisions with a right answer that was obvious in retrospect. This one argues the hard part is precisely that no such answer exists.
books.misses: Read as war stories, but the structure is the argument: the book spends its length on situations where all options are bad because that is the claim.
books.apply: Take a decision you have been postponing and write out the least-bad option rather than the right one.
books.verify: Quote is from the book. Confirm wording.
takeaways: There are no silver bullets. Most progress comes from lead bullets fired for a long time.
Tell people the truth about the situation. They already suspect it.
Take care of the people, the product and the profits, in that order.
The hardest decisions have no good option. Choose the least bad one and own it.
There is no formula for the hard things. Anyone selling one has not run anything hard.

books.title: Deep Work
books.author: Cal Newport
books.quote: Clarity about what matters provides clarity about what does not.
books.core_idea: Sustained, distraction-free concentration is both increasingly rare and increasingly valuable, and it is a trainable capacity rather than a personality trait.
books.tension: Focus or flexibility? The book takes a hard position that a great deal of modern work is shallow by design, which does not survive contact with every job.
books.misses: Summaries take the productivity advice and skip the economic argument about why the skill is becoming scarce.
books.apply: Block ninety minutes tomorrow with the phone in another room and notice how long it takes before you want it.
books.verify: Quote appears in the book. Confirm wording.
takeaways: Depth is trainable, not a personality trait. Concentration improves the way endurance does.
Schedule shallow work into a box rather than letting it fill the gaps.
Boredom is practice. If you reach for the phone in every queue, focus has nowhere to grow.
Quit a tool for thirty days and only reinstate it if its absence actually cost you something.
Ritual beats motivation: same place, same hours, same start, no negotiation.

books.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
books.author: Daniel Kahneman
books.quote: Nothing in life is as important as you think it is while you are thinking about it.
books.core_idea: Two systems drive thought: one fast, automatic and confident; one slow, effortful and lazy. Most errors come from the fast one being trusted for work it cannot do.
books.tension: Knowing about a bias does very little to prevent it. The book is unusually honest that awareness is not a cure.
books.misses: It is used as a list of biases to name in arguments. Kahneman's own point is that you will not catch your own in real time.
books.apply: Next time you feel certain, ask what evidence would change your mind. If nothing would, the certainty is not about the evidence.
books.verify: Quote is the focusing illusion, widely printed. Confirm wording.
takeaways: Confidence is a feeling produced by coherence, not by evidence. They come apart constantly.
What you can recall easily feels more common than it is. Vividness is not frequency.
You judge a whole experience by its peak and its end, not by its average.
Losses land about twice as hard as equivalent gains, which explains most reluctance.
Knowing a bias does not disarm it. Build the check into the process, not the moment.

books.title: Sapiens
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.quote: Fiction has enabled us not merely to imagine things, but to do so collectively.
books.core_idea: Large-scale human cooperation runs on shared imagined orders - money, nations, companies, rights - that exist because enough people act as if they do.
books.tension: The book is strongest as narrative and weakest where it compresses contested history into a clean line. That is exactly what makes it readable.
books.misses: The cognitive revolution chapter gets quoted; the argument about agriculture as a trap is the more provocative claim.
books.apply: Pick something you treat as objectively real at work - a title, a target, a process - and ask what holds it up.
books.notable: Included on Barack Obama's published summer reading list, and publicly recommended by Bill Gates on his blog.
books.verify: Both references are documented publicly. Confirm the specific year and wording before citing.

books.title: Zero to One
books.author: Peter Thiel
books.quote: What important truth do very few people agree with you on?
books.core_idea: Real progress comes from going from nothing to something, not from copying what works. Competition is often evidence that you are not doing anything new.
books.tension: The argument for monopoly as a goal is genuinely contested, and the book knows it.
books.misses: Read as a startup playbook. It is closer to a philosophy of what counts as progress.
books.apply: Answer the question in the quote honestly, in writing. Most people find they do not have an answer.
books.verify: This is the book's central interview question. Confirm wording.
takeaways: Going from nothing to something beats copying what already works.
Competition is often evidence you are not doing anything new.
Ask what important truth very few people agree with you on, and answer it in writing.
Start by monopolising a small market you can actually own, then widen.
Sales and distribution decide outcomes far more than founders who love the product want to believe.

books.title: Never Split the Difference
books.author: Chris Voss
books.quote: Never be so sure of what you want that you wouldn't take something better.
books.core_idea: Negotiation is emotional information-gathering, not logical trading. Understanding what the other person actually needs beats arguing for what you want.
books.tension: Tactics learned from hostage negotiation can read as manipulation in ordinary relationships, and the book's own framing does not fully resolve that.
books.misses: The tactical labels get repeated. The underlying claim - that people need to feel heard before they can move - is the part that generalises.
books.apply: In the next disagreement, say what you think the other person wants before saying what you want.
books.verify: Quote is from the book. Confirm wording.
takeaways: Say what you think the other person wants before you say what you want.
Label the emotion out loud. Naming it lowers it.
"No" is the start of a negotiation, not the end of one.
Get to "that's right" — agreement is meaningless until they feel understood.
Never be so certain of what you want that you would refuse something better.

books.title: Mindset
books.author: Carol S. Dweck
books.core_idea: Whether people treat ability as fixed or developable changes what they do after failing, which over time changes what they become capable of.
books.tension: The idea has been diluted into praise-the-effort advice, and Dweck herself has publicly pushed back on that reading.
books.misses: A growth mindset is not optimism about outcomes. It is a claim about what you do after a specific failure.
books.apply: Recall your last failure and note whether your explanation was about capacity or about method.
books.verify: Quote is from the book. Dweck's later comments on misapplication are publicly documented - confirm before citing them.
takeaways: The question is not whether you failed. It is what you conclude about yourself when you do.
Praise the method, not the talent. Talent praise teaches people to avoid hard things.
"Not yet" is a different sentence from "not able", and it changes what happens next.
Effort without a change in strategy is not growth mindset. It is repetition.
Choosing tasks you might fail at is the actual behaviour. The belief on its own does nothing.

books.title: The Intelligent Investor
books.author: Benjamin Graham
books.quote: The investor's chief problem, and even his worst enemy, is likely to be himself.
books.core_idea: Investing is the discipline of paying less than something is worth and refusing to be moved by price movements that carry no information.
books.tension: Value discipline is simple to state and extremely hard to hold through a decade when it underperforms.
books.misses: The formulas date badly. The chapters on the investor's temperament do not.
books.apply: Write down what would make you sell something you own before you need to decide it.
books.notable: Warren Buffett has repeatedly and publicly described it as the best book on investing ever written, and has cited chapters 8 and 20 specifically.
books.verify: Buffett's recommendation is extensively documented in Berkshire letters and interviews. Confirm the exact phrasing you attribute to him.

books.title: Meditations
books.author: Marcus Aurelius
books.quote: You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.
books.quote_note: Heavily translation-dependent, and this rendering is disputed by some scholars. Attribute to a translation, or choose a passage from the edition you own.
books.core_idea: A private notebook of a working ruler reminding himself, repeatedly, of the same few things - which is itself the lesson about how principles are held.
books.tension: It is read as calm wisdom; it is closer to a man arguing with himself because the argument keeps needing to be had again.
books.misses: Quote pages flatten it into serenity. The repetition is the substance.
books.apply: Write the same instruction to yourself three days running and notice whether you needed to.
books.verify: Check the translation. This particular rendering is contested - safest to quote your own edition.

books.title: Good to Great
books.author: Jim Collins
books.quote: Good is the enemy of great.
books.core_idea: Sustained excellence came less from dramatic strategy than from disciplined people, disciplined thought and disciplined action, applied over long periods.
books.tension: Several of the companies studied later struggled badly, which is either a fatal problem for the method or the most interesting thing about it.
books.misses: The famous concepts get repeated without the survivorship critique, which is the more useful discussion.
books.apply: Name one thing your team is good at that is preventing it from being excellent at something else.
books.verify: Quote is the book's opening line. The later performance of the studied companies is publicly documented - confirm specifics before citing.

books.title: Start with Why
books.author: Simon Sinek
books.quote: People don't buy what you do; they buy why you do it.
books.core_idea: Organisations that can state their purpose plainly communicate from the inside out, and that ordering changes what people remember.
books.tension: The claim is stated far more confidently than the evidence supports, which is worth saying out loud when recommending it.
books.misses: It is treated as a marketing formula. It is closer to a claim about clarity of belief.
books.apply: Write your work's why in one sentence without using the words quality, innovative or customer-focused.
books.verify: Quote is the book's central line. Confirm wording.

books.title: Essentialism
books.author: Greg McKeown
books.quote: If you don't prioritize your life, someone else will.
books.core_idea: The disciplined pursuit of less: deciding deliberately where to spend effort, and treating most opportunities as costs rather than gains.
books.tension: Easy to state, and largely unavailable to people whose work is assigned rather than chosen.
books.misses: Read as a productivity system. The harder argument is about the social cost of declining things.
books.apply: Decline one thing this week and say plainly that you are declining it, rather than going quiet.
books.verify: Quote is from the book. Confirm wording.
takeaways: If you do not prioritise your life, someone else will.
Almost everything is noise. Treat opportunities as costs, not as gains.
A slow yes beats a fast one. Buy time before committing.
Say the decline plainly. Going quiet is worse than saying no.
Protect the asset. The person doing the work is the thing that breaks first.

books.title: Outliers
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell
books.quote: Practice isn't the thing you do once you're good. It's the thing you do that makes you good.
books.core_idea: Exceptional success is far more dependent on timing, culture, and accumulated advantage than the stories we tell about individuals allow.
books.tension: The ten-thousand-hours claim has been substantially contested by the researcher whose work it drew on.
books.misses: The hours figure travelled; the argument about birth dates, timing and inherited advantage is the more durable part.
books.apply: Take a success you attribute to your own effort and list three conditions you did not create.
books.notable: Anders Ericsson, whose research the ten-thousand-hour idea draws on, publicly disputed the popularised version.
books.verify: Ericsson's disagreement is documented in his own writing. Confirm before citing him.
